text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave power station with about 1,300W or more of surge output. Choose roughly 1,000-1,500Wh for 12-24 hours, or 2,000Wh or more if you want a cushion or a multi-day outage.

## Check these three things

1. **Surge watts (the one that most often fails).** The compressor spikes at startup. Sources put it at about 1,000-1,200W for a typical fridge and up to 2,400W for large or older ones. Look for a surge rating of at least 1,300W, and more if your fridge is big or old. [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)
2. **Continuous watts.** A fridge runs at roughly 100-250W, so almost any 1,000W-class station covers it. Add anything else you'll run at the same time. [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)
3. **Watt-hours (runtime).** The compressor only runs about a third of the time, so average draw is much lower than the label wattage. One estimate for an 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge is about 41W average, or about 1,400Wh per day after inverter losses and 20% headroom. [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator) Other sources estimate 50-70W average, which is somewhat higher.

## Rough sizing

| Outage length | Capacity to look for |
|---|---|
| ~12 hours | ~800-1,000Wh |
| ~24 hours | ~1,400-2,000Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800Wh+ |

You can calculate your own number from the yellow EnergyGuide label: kWh per year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 gives average watts. Multiply by hours, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, then add about 20% margin. [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator) A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average twice that figure, and a warm kitchen or frequent door opening pushes it up too. Keep the door shut during the outage.

## Options from these sources

- **BLUETTI AC200L (2,048Wh, 2,400W, expandable):** lists at $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF according to the retailer's test. Buy it here: [Dealectric listing](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l). This is an affiliate link, and Dealectric earns a commission. It's a good fit if you want a day or more of runtime, or room to add batteries later.
- **Anker SOLIX S2000 (2,010Wh, 1,500W, 3,000W peak, pure sine wave):** listed at $699.99 after coupon. See it here: [Anker SOLIX guide and product link](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator). The link goes to Anker's guide page, which has the shop button.
- **BLUETTI AC180 (1,152Wh, 1,800W, 2,700W peak) and Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (~1,070Wh):** these suit a smaller, roughly half-day to one-day setup. Prices are about $399-699 for the AC180 and $449-799 for the Jackery. Both are described in [BlackBox Supplies' guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), and HomeGrid HQ estimates about 17 hours for the Jackery ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). I only have those guide pages, not direct product links, so check current prices before buying.

Avoid small power banks and compact units. Many fail the surge check, and you want pure sine wave output for a compressor motor.

To narrow this down, tell me your fridge's size, whether it has an ice maker, how long an outage you want to cover, and whether you need to power anything else, like a freezer or modem.
